939.title: Gujrat and annexation, 1849
939.hook: the last battle is lost, the soldiers lay down their arms, and the Punjab is annexed
939.howItsDone: Sikh histories mark the defeat at Gujrat and the annexation that followed as the end of the Sikh kingdom of the Punjab, and the story of the soldiers laying down their arms is still told at gatherings about that history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chillianwala, and your line was they held. Today, the holding ends.

A line of soldiers comes forward, one by one, and lays its weapons on a pile: swords, matchlocks, shields. These are men of the Khalsa army, and the war is over. A story is told about that day. An old soldier, setting down his arms, says quietly that today Ranjit Singh has died. The Maharaja was long dead. But the kingdom he built was ending in front of them.
screen: `WEAPONS LAID ON A PILE.` → `TODAY RANJIT SINGH HAS DIED.` → `A KINGDOM ENDING.`

segments.voice: Gujrat here is a town in the Punjab, not the Indian state with a similar name. After Chillianwala, the British waited for more troops, and above all more heavy guns. At Gujrat they used them: a long, heavy bombardment came before the infantry moved, and this time the Sikh line broke. The British pursued the retreating army. Its leaders, Sher Singh Attariwala and his father Chattar Singh, gave themselves up, and the soldiers handed over their arms. That's where the old soldier's story is set. It may be remembered more than recorded, but Sikhs keep telling it because it says what the day meant. Lord Dalhousie did not restore the court at Lahore. He declared the Punjab part of British India. The boy Maharaja, Duleep Singh, still a child, was made to put his name to terms that gave up his kingdom and his claims to it. The flag over the fort at Lahore was changed. Near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, in his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person whose strength has gone, who is bound and can find no way out. In the next breath the verse turns: strength returns, the bonds fall away, and everything is in the Lord's hands. The Guru doesn't pretend the binding isn't real. He just doesn't stop the verse there. A kingdom did end at Gujrat, and the old soldier's story doesn't hide it.

940.title: The diamond sent away
940.hook: the Koh-i-Noor is taken from the boy king and sent to Queen Victoria
940.howItsDone: The Koh-i-Noor remains in the British crown jewels, and in Sikh tellings of the annexation it stands for everything taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh as a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bandhan, and your line was the kingdom ended. Today, a stone that stood for that kingdom leaves it.

A small box, and inside it a single great diamond. Ranjit Singh wore it on his arm at court. Afghan rulers held it before him, and Mughal emperors before them. Its name, the Koh-i-Noor, is usually given in English as the mountain of light. When the Punjab was annexed, the terms said this stone would go to the Queen of England. It was taken from a boy who was still a child.
screen: `A STONE IN A SMALL BOX.` → `WORN ON A MAHARAJA'S ARM.` → `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Koh-i-Noor had passed from ruler to ruler, often by force. Ranjit Singh obtained it from an Afghan king, Shah Shuja, who had come to him as a refugee, and the circumstances are still argued over. At Lahore it became a sign of the kingdom itself. When Lord Dalhousie annexed the Punjab, the agreement named the Koh-i-Noor and said it was to be surrendered to the Queen. Dalhousie wanted it sent as a prize of the war, not as a gift from the Maharaja. A story is told in the life of John Lawrence, one of the officers then governing the Punjab: the stone was handed to him in its little box, he slipped it into a pocket and forgot it, and when he was asked for it he had a bad moment searching. Then it went under guard to the coast and by ship to Britain. There it was cut down to a new shape and became part of the crown jewels. Its return has been asked for, from more than one country, and the question is still open. In Sikh tellings, the diamond isn't really about wealth. It's about a child who lost his kingdom and then lost its sign too. Guru Nanak, in a hymn tradition links to the invasion of Babur, says that for the sake of wealth many were ruined and disgraced; it can't be gathered without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go with you when you die.

941.title: The boy far from home
941.hook: Duleep Singh, still a child, is raised by British guardians and baptized a Christian
941.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell Duleep Singh's childhood under British guardianship as part of the loss of the kingdom, and his baptism is read differently in different accounts: as his own choice, or as the result of being separated from his mother and his faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, moh, and your line was taken away. Today, the boy the diamond was taken from.

A garden by the Ganges at Fatehgarh, a long way from Lahore. A boy with a pony, a tutor, a few servants, and a Scottish doctor who has been put in charge of him. The boy has been a Maharaja. He has sat on his father's throne, been bowed to by generals, worn the jewels of the Punjab. Now he has lessons, a garden and guardians. His mother has been sent away, and the court he knew is gone.
screen: `A GARDEN AT FATEHGARH.` → `A BOY WHO WAS A MAHARAJA.` → `LESSONS, AND GUARDIANS.`

segments.voice: After the annexation, Duleep Singh was placed in the care of Dr. John Login, who had looked after the treasury at Lahore. Login and his wife, Lena, raised him. Her later book about the boy is warm toward him, and also plainly written from the guardians' side. He was taken out of the Punjab to Fatehgarh, away from the Sikh court, the gurdwaras of Lahore, and anyone who might raise him as a Sikh king. The British saw a boy who could become a rallying point, so they kept him far away. In those years, a boy in his early teens, Duleep Singh asked to become a Christian, and he was baptized. The Login account says the wish was his own, that he'd been listening to a household servant read from the Bible. Some Sikh writers see it differently: a child cut off from his mother, his faith and his people, shaped by the only adults left around him. Both readings are still held, and the sources can't fully settle what was in a child's heart. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Bilaval, the Guru says the hot wind does not touch the one who shelters in the Lord: a protecting line is drawn on every side, and no pain comes near. Those words were there all along, in the scripture of the faith he was raised away from.

942.title: An English country house
942.hook: Duleep lives as a gentleman in Suffolk, far from the Punjab
942.howItsDone: Elveden Hall in Suffolk is remembered in Sikh history as Duleep Singh's English home, and Sikh visitors to Britain sometimes travel there to see the place where Maharaja Duleep Singh lived.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sarnai, and your line was a boy far away. Today, the boy is grown, and further away than ever.

Shotguns crack across a cold, sandy heath in Suffolk. Beaters walk the fields, birds go up, and the gentlemen fire. The host of the shooting party is known as a remarkable shot. He owns the house, the woods and the land around it. He dines with the Prince of Wales and has been received by Queen Victoria. And he was born a Maharaja of the Punjab.
screen: `SHOTGUNS OVER A SUFFOLK HEATH.` → `THE HOST IS A FINE SHOT.` → `BORN A MAHARAJA.`

segments.voice: In his teens, Duleep Singh was brought to Britain. The Queen took an interest in him, and he was welcomed at court as an exotic and charming guest. He lived on an allowance from the government that had taken his kingdom, and it was never as much as he thought was owed. He bought an estate called Elveden, in Suffolk, and rebuilt the hall. Inside, some rooms were made to look like an Indian palace, with carved arches and rich ornament, in the middle of the English countryside. Outside, he turned the land into a great shooting estate. He married Bamba Müller, who had grown up in Cairo, and their children were raised as English gentry. He shot, entertained, spent heavily and fell into debt. From the outside, the picture was complete: an English gentleman with an Indian title. But the rooms that looked like a palace tell their own story. A man who had everything a country house can offer still built a piece of the home he had lost into its walls. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, which tradition says was written in longing for the Guru's presence, he says his mind yearns for the sight of the Guru, crying out like the rainbird crying for rain, and that he can't sleep or rest without it. Some Sikh readers of Duleep's story hear that ache in the Indian rooms at Elveden.

943.title: Mother and son again, 1861
943.hook: after long years apart, Duleep meets his mother, and she tells him of his heritage
943.carry: she told him who he was
943.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Maharani Jind Kaur as a mother who never stopped resisting the loss of her son and her kingdom, and the meeting in Calcutta is told as the moment Duleep Singh began to recover his heritage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elveden, and your line was far from punjab. Today, someone arrives who remembers.

What do you say to a mother you last saw when you were small? A hotel in Calcutta. A grown man in English clothes waits in a room. The door opens, and a woman comes in, older than he remembers, her eyesight failing. She is Maharani Jind Kaur, the queen who was sent away. When she reaches him, the story goes, she runs her hands over his head, looking for his uncut hair, and finds it cut short.
screen: `A HOTEL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A QUEEN WHOSE EYES ARE FAILING.` → `HER HANDS ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: After she was separated from her son, Jind Kaur was held as a prisoner. She escaped in disguise and made her way to Nepal, where she lived in exile under the protection of its rulers. All those years, letters between mother and son were watched or stopped. Duleep Singh asked to see her, and in time the British allowed it, as long as she did not go back to the Punjab. They met in Calcutta. The boy she had last held was now a grown man, a Christian, living as an English gentleman. She came with him to England and lived near him in London. She talked to him about the Punjab, about his father, Ranjit Singh, about the kingdom and how it was lost, and about the Sikh faith he had been raised away from. Histories that follow his life mark this as the moment something in him began to turn. There's a hymn of Guru Arjan in which a mother speaks to her son: this is your mother's blessing, son, that you never forget the Lord for even an instant. That blessing is about remembering the Lord. In Calcutta, and then in London, this mother's gift was a remembering too: she gave her son back the story of who he was.

944.title: Jind Kaur's death, 1863
944.hook: she dies in London, and her son takes her ashes toward India
944.howItsDone: At a Sikh funeral, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are placed in flowing water; Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories and gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asees, and your line was she told him who he was. Today, that mother's last journey.

In a rented house in Kensington, with London's carriages passing in the street, a queen of the Punjab is dying. She has been a regent, a prisoner, a fugitive across the hills to Nepal, and, at the end, a mother living near her son. She will not see Lahore again. And when she dies, her son faces a question no English gentleman is trained for: how do you take your mother home?
screen: `A RENTED HOUSE IN KENSINGTON.` → `A QUEEN WHO WON'T SEE LAHORE.` → `HOW DO YOU TAKE HER HOME?`

segments.voice: Jind Kaur lived near Duleep Singh in London after their meeting in Calcutta. Her health was poor and her sight was failing, but she kept telling him about the Punjab, and the histories suggest the stories took hold. She died in London, far from the land she had ruled as regent. Sikh custom is to cremate the body. In Victorian London that was not a simple thing to arrange, and her son wanted her rites done in India, not in England. So he took his mother's body by sea toward India. But he was not permitted to take her into the Punjab. She was cremated on the banks of the Godavari river at Nasik, far to the south of the land she had known, and a small memorial was built there. Her ashes, tradition says, were later moved to Lahore and laid near her husband's memorial, though that came long afterward. In the Alahniyan, the songs of mourning by Guru Nanak in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that whoever has come must rise and go, and that this world is a passing show. At a Sikh funeral the hymns are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are given to flowing water. A son who had been raised far from all of it did what he could to carry his mother home, and got as close as he was allowed.

945.title: Duleep returns to Sikhi, 1886
945.hook: stopped at Aden on his way to India, he takes amrit again
945.howItsDone: Sikhs take amrit, the Khalsa initiation, in a ceremony led by initiated Sikhs, and Duleep Singh's initiation at Aden is remembered as his return to the faith of his parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alahniyan, and your line was ashes carried home. Today, her son tries to go home himself.

Officials climb aboard a steamer that has just tied up at a hot, rocky port where ships bound for India stop to take on coal. They have orders for one of the passengers: he may go no further. The port is Aden. The passenger, traveling east with his family, is Duleep Singh. He has left England and set out for India, and he has told the Sikhs he is coming. He will never reach them. But in this port, something happens anyway.
screen: `A COALING PORT CALLED ADEN.` → `ORDERS: NO FURTHER.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: After his mother's stories, Duleep Singh began to read about the Sikh faith and about the annexation. He came to believe the terms that took his kingdom were unjust, and that the British owed him more than his allowance. He grew bitter, and he decided to go back to India and to the faith of his father. He set out by sea, writing openly to the Sikhs that he was returning to them. The British government did not want him in India, where he might become a rallying point, so he was stopped at Aden. There, in a foreign port, he took amrit, the Khalsa initiation, from Sikhs who had come for it. The man who had been baptized a Christian as a boy was initiated as a Sikh as a grown man. He never reached the Punjab. But he had come back. In the Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das opens with a cry of joy addressed to his mother: joy has come, mother, for I have found the true Guru. A mother who told her son who he was, and a son who came back to it, in the place where he was told he could go no further. Look back at the week: bandhan, moh, the boy at Fatehgarh, the house in Suffolk, a mother found again and then lost. All week the story has moved away from the Punjab. Today, in the port where he was stopped, it turns toward it.
screen: `THE TURN TOWARD HOME.` · `STOPPED AT ADEN.` · `AMRIT IN A FOREIGN PORT.` · `JOY HAS COME, MOTHER.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`
